doctrine: Brand is the gut feeling customers have about you when absent: the internal reputation shaped by every touchpoint (product, messaging, packaging, behavior, response time). Brand cannot be directly controlled—only influenced. Product quality is table stakes; identity (what you stand for, who your tribe is, why they choose you over cheaper alternatives) is the defensible moat. DO NOT sell features; sell belonging and aspirational identity ('I'm a Stanley girl'). Core mechanics: (1) Design identity BEFORE design elements. Define psychographics (values, lifestyle), specific problem solved, non-negotiable values, desired gut feeling (3 words), the enemy/villain. (2) Validation sequence: Design → Sample (1-2 units) → Social proof test (posts/DMs) → Influencer seeding (10-20 micro accounts under 50K followers; higher engagement) → Email/SMS waitlist target 500+ → Drop to list first → Organic revenue threshold triggers scale. Never mass-produce without proof. (3) Manufacturing: Tech pack (1-4 page spec doc with mockup, size chart, graphic placement, materials, care). Supplier vetting via Trade Assurance. 4-stage payment (25/25/25/25): deposit, materials in-house, production complete, pre-shipment video. Revision briefs use visual markup (circles/arrows/text overlays on photos), NOT text descriptions. (4) Content launch (THCPP): Tease (BTS design/samples) → Hype (lifestyle context, not flat-lay) → Collect (email/SMS signup) → Push (list-first drop, limited stock, urgency) → Pull (retarget with paid ads using proven organic content). (5) Scale winners, not trends. When organic revenue exceeds 10K, add 8+ colorways and 2+ garment variations of the winner. Never discount. If demand is low, product or story is wrong, not price. Scarcity manufactures desire. (6) Community beats advertising. Founder story documented daily (gritty, failing, building in public) is the brand narrative. Every piece of content is a strategic asset. (7) Marketing anchor (non-negotiable rule: never discount / never stock photography / never mass retail) prevents discount dilution and brand equity erosion. (8) Growth stages: 0-10K (organic, PMF, manual outreach, content velocity; skip paid ads/rebrands); 10-50K (paid ads on proven content, SMS/email automation, variation scaling, first hire); 50-100K (SOPs, team, wholesale, CRO; stop micromanaging); 100K+ (leadership, delegation, high-tier hiring, brand equity positioning). (9) The 3% Rule: improve proven products 3% for specific audience rather than inventing. (10) Print-on-Demand path for zero-capital launch: Shopify + POD (Printful/Tapstitch), auto-fulfill, validate before bulk. Lower margins, zero risk. Never sell what you haven't held. (11) Compound improvement loop: publish → review against last version → identify one 10% improvement → repeat. 100 reps builds an untouchable brand; most quit at rep 7.

workflows: 1. Brand Identity Foundation: Define psychographics (values/lifestyle) -> specific problem solved -> non-negotiable values -> 3-word gut feeling -> enemy/villain

2. Visual System Expression: Name (trademark check) -> Logo (3 distinct directions) -> Mood board (emotional territory) -> Typography/Color (recognition) -> Brand Gap test (survey 10 people, compare to mission)

3. Validation-First Launch: Design (3% Rule improvement) -> Sample (1-2 units) -> Social proof test (saves/shares/DMs) -> Influencer seeding (10-20 micro) -> Collect interest (500+ signups) -> Drop to list (7-day fulfillment)
4. Supply Chain Setup: Tech pack (mockup + specs) -> Supplier vetting (Trade Assurance + video proof) -> 4-stage payments (25/25/25/25) -> Revision briefs (visual markup only)
5. THCPP Launch Sequence: Tease (BTS/fabric/samples) -> Hype (lifestyle context) -> Collect (email/SMS) -> Push (list-first drop + urgency) -> Pull (retarget with paid ads)
6. Scale Winners Strategy: Identify 10K+ organic revenue product -> Stop inventing -> Add 8+ colorways -> Expand to 2+ garment types -> Reinvest 50% into paid ads with proven organic content
7. Brand Protection Loop: Establish marketing anchor (non-negotiable rule) -> Filter every decision through anchor -> Kill revenue-positive moves that conflict -> Repeat at every scale stage
prompts: Who is this brand for? Define by psychographics (values, lifestyle, aspirations), not demographics.
What specific problem does this solve? (Not 'I make clothes.' But 'women who can never find pants that fit.')
What do you stand for? What do you refuse to do? What are non-negotiable values?
What is the 3-word gut feeling you want people to have about your brand?
Who is the enemy? Name the industry standard you're fighting against.
Does this product or story decision strengthen or weaken the brand?
Is this move aligned with our marketing anchor (the one non-negotiable rule)?
What identity does our customer currently have vs. their aspirational identity? How is our product the bridge?
Does this make us easier to say no to (or harder)?
Is this move short-term revenue at the cost of long-term brand equity?

contradictions: None detected. The playbook maintains internal consistency across branding, operations, and psychology frameworks.
weird_gold: The Brand Gap test: Survey 10 random people for 3 words describing your brand, compare to your internal mission. The gap is your work.
The markup revolution: Revision briefs using visual overlays (circles/arrows on photos) convert success rates dramatically vs. text instructions—universal language across manufacturers.
Micro-influencer arbitrage: 10-20 accounts under 50K followers generate higher engagement than 1 celebrity account; cost near-zero (product seeding vs. paid sponsorship).
The 3% Rule as a scaling law: Refining a proven product 3% for your specific tribe costs 10% of R&D vs. inventing new SKUs; converts 3x higher because market already validated the base product.
Compound improvement at rep 50: By 50 reps of the loop (publish-review-improve-repeat), you're unrecognizable to yourself. By rep 100, you're untouchable. Data point: most founders quit at rep 7.

Print-on-Demand as a validation tool: You physically hold the product BEFORE you sell it. POD removes inventory risk but lower margins act as a forcing function: only scale winners (10K+ organic revenue) to bulk manufacturing.

Marketing anchor as anti-fragility: One non-negotiable rule ('never discount,' 'never stock photography,' 'never mass-retail') prevents 100 small brand-erosion decisions per year. Short-term revenue temptations are automatically filtered.

The founder story is the moat: In a market where anyone can make a decent garment, documented vulnerability and sacrifice build an information asymmetry that price-cutting cannot compete against. The mess IS credibility.
